elements.quote: This systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of ER behavioral observation and physiological measures of children and adolescents, including their theoretical embedding and psychometric properties.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: Valid and reliable ER measures are needed to develop models for mental health promotion and treatment. This systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of ER behavioral observation and physiological measures of children and adolescents, including their theoretical embedding and psychometric properties.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective of the review.

elements.quote: We included empirical studies assessing ER as an outcome variable in children and adolescents aged 0-15 years using at least one behavioral or physiological ER measure. Studies on secondary literature were excluded.
elements.reason: Main inclusion and exclusion criteria are specified in the abstract.

elements.quote: Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic literature search in PubMed, PsycINFO, Psyndex plus, and Web of Science without language restrictions.
elements.reason: Information sources are named, but the abstract does not report when each source was last searched (the date 13.09.2024 appears only in the main text, text_10).
The abstract does not mention any risk of bias assessment methods; these are described only in the main text (text_11).

elements.quote: Measurement types, theoretical grounding, and psychometric properties (reliability, validity, objectivity) were extracted and compared across age groups using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the synthesis methods used.

elements.quote: A total of 516 studies met inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of included studies and some characteristics, but does not report the total number of participants.

elements.quote: Only 5% reported validity evidence, 62% reliability, and 20% objectivity. Few studies referenced an ER definition or empirically tested an ER model.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes (psychometric property reporting, measures used, group differences).

elements.quote: the proportion reporting reliability measure was 63.7% (95% CI [61.8, 65.6], k = 314)
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted (per main text), but the abstract does not report any summary estimate with confidence/credible interval.

elements.quote: Behavioral observation was more frequently used in younger children, whereas physiological measures were more common in older children ( p < .001; V = .37).
elements.reason: When groups are compared, the abstract indicates the direction of the difference (which group is favored/more common).
The abstract does not summarize limitations of the included evidence such as risk of bias, inconsistency, or imprecision; limitations appear only in the main text (text_32).

elements.quote: Conclusion ER measurement in children and adolescents is characterized by limited psychometric reporting and insufficient theoretical integration. This review provides an overview of available methods and their psychometric properties, facilitating the selection of appropriate measures for future research.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and their implications.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide the register name or registration number; PROSPERO registration (CRD42021266452) appears only in the main text (text_6).

elements.quote: Emotion regulation (ER) is crucial for understanding mental health and disorders. Valid and reliable ER measures are needed to develop models for mental health promotion and treatment.
elements.reason: The abstract background briefly indicates the state of knowledge (ER is important; measures lack validity/reliability reporting), but the retrieved evidence does not include the Introduction's fuller description of existing knowledge and uncertainties (checklist points to p. 6, which is not retrieved).

elements.quote: Valid and reliable ER measures are needed to develop models for mental health promotion and treatment. This systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of ER behavioral observation and physiological measures of children and adolescents, including their theoretical embedding and psychometric properties.
elements.reason: The need for the review is stated in the abstract (need for valid/reliable ER measures and a comprehensive overview), but the full rationale in the Introduction is not among the retrieved evidence.
No retrieved evidence discusses prior similar systematic reviews or explains how the current review updates or differs from them.
This is a review of assessment/measurement methods for emotion regulation, not a review of intervention effects, so a mechanism of action is not required.
The review addresses measurement methods rather than complex interventions or delivery contexts, so a logic model of intervention components is not applicable.

No retrieved evidence contains an explicit statement of the review's objective(s) or question(s) using a question-formulation framework. The only related evidence is a completed PRISMA abstract checklist marking 'Objectives' as 'yes' (table_6), which is a self-assessment, not the actual objective statement, and the abstract fragment (text_3) only mentions the need for multimethod approaches without stating the review's objectives.

elements.quote: Studies were required to use at least one ER measurement and report ER as an outcome variable. Both studies with and without group comparisons were eligible.
elements.reason: This is a systematic review of assessment/measurement methods, not a review of intervention effects, so planned intervention comparisons in PICO form do not apply. Eligibility was instead based on PICOS criteria for study inclusion.

elements.quote: Studies were included according to the PICOS criteria [177]. Eligible studies included participants from birth to 15 years and 11 months. Studies were required to use at least one ER measurement and report ER as an outcome variable. Both studies with and without group comparisons were eligible.
elements.reason: Eligibility criteria specify the framework (PICOS), population age range, required outcome/measurement, and eligible study designs (group comparisons allowed; secondary literature excluded).

elements.quote: No language restrictions were applied; studies in all languages were included. Studies reporting on secondary literature (e.g. meta-analyses, reviews) were excluded.
elements.reason: Language and publication status (secondary literature excluded) are reported, but no dissemination year restriction (or explicit statement of none) is specified in the eligibility criteria.

elements.quote: Other exclusions were based on ineligible age groups, absence of an ER outcome measure, secondary data, or insufficient detail on ER measurement.
elements.reason: The review does not distinguish exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported; 'insufficient detail on ER measurement' is not clearly differentiated.

elements.quote: Measurement types, theoretical grounding, and psychometric properties (reliability, validity, objectivity) were extracted and compared across age groups using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests.
elements.reason: Synthesis groups (measurement types, age groups) are implied in the abstract, but the Methods/eligibility section does not explicitly specify and link the grouping of studies for each synthesis to the review objectives.

elements.quote: We initially preregistered an age range of 0 to 18 years. However, this age range was reduced to 0 to 15 years and 11 months due to the large number of eligible records identified.
elements.reason: A rationale is provided for the notable restriction of the age range from 0-18 to 0-15 years and 11 months.

elements.quote: The search was updated continuously until 13.09.2024.
elements.reason: A last search date (13.09.2024) is reported for the databases searched.

elements.quote: We used topic-specific databases PubMed (including MEDLINE; Ovid), PsycINFO (including PsycArticles; EBSCOhost), Psyndex plus (EBSCOhost) and Web of Science (Thomson Reuters, Clarivate Analytics) for adjoining disciplines. ... No publication date limits were applied.
elements.reason: Database names and platforms/interfaces are reported, and coverage dates are addressed by stating no publication date limits were applied; however, database coverage start dates are not explicitly given.

elements.quote: In contrast to the previously pre-registered search strategy, the Google Scholar database was excluded due to the large number of records retrieved
elements.reason: No study registers or online repositories were searched; Google Scholar was explicitly excluded, so this requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: the Google Scholar database was excluded due to the large number of records retrieved, which exceeded the feasible scope of screening
elements.reason: No websites or search engines were searched; Google Scholar was excluded, so this requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: For studies with unavailable full-texts, authors were contacted or articles purchased.
elements.reason: Authors were contacted only for full-text retrieval, not to identify studies; no organisations or manufacturers were contacted for study identification.

elements.quote: For studies with unavailable full-texts, authors were contacted or articles purchased.
elements.reason: No individuals were contacted to identify studies; author contact was only for obtaining full texts.

elements.quote: Additionally, manual reference checks and citation tracking in the Social Science Citation Index were conducted.
elements.reason: Reference list examination (manual reference checks) is specified.

elements.quote: manual reference checks and citation tracking in the Social Science Citation Index were conducted
elements.reason: The citation index (Social Science Citation Index) is named and the overall search end date (13.09.2024) applies, but seed reports for backward/forward citation searching are not specified.

elements.quote: We used topic-specific databases PubMed (including MEDLINE; Ovid), PsycINFO (including PsycArticles; EBSCOhost), Psyndex plus (EBSCOhost) and Web of Science (Thomson Reuters, Clarivate Analytics)
elements.reason: No journals or conference proceedings were hand-searched as sources; only bibliographic databases, reference checks, and citation tracking were used.

elements.quote: The search strategy was piloted in PubMed and adapted for each database (search strategy for PubMed, Appendix, File 3). ... We used topic-specific databases PubMed (including MEDLINE; Ovid), PsycINFO (including PsycArticles; EBSCOhost), Psyndex plus (EBSCOhost) and Web of Science ... Additionally, manual reference checks and citation tracking in the Social Science Citation Index were conducted.
elements.reason: Databases, supplementary methods, and a reference to the full PubMed strategy (Appendix File 3) are reported, and File 3 shows the core search terms, but the complete strategy as actually run for each database is not fully reproduced in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: No publication date limits were applied.
elements.reason: Date limits are explicitly described (none applied), and an age filter is shown in File 3 ('If there is no age selection by the searching machine, we add: AND child* OR ...'), but limits are not explicitly justified by reference to the eligibility criteria.
No citation of published search approaches or filters, or description of adaptations, is present in the retrieved evidence.
No natural-language processing or text-analysis tools for identifying or refining search terms are reported.
No tools for translating search strings between sources are reported.
No validation of the search strategy is described in the retrieved evidence.
No peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) is described.
No description of the conceptual structure used to develop the search (if not PICO-based) is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently screened by two authors (MB, RD) and two advanced graduate students... All potentially eligible articles were independently assessed in full text by three authors (MB, RD, FS) and two advanced graduate students.
elements.reason: The number of reviewers is specified for both title/abstract screening and full-text assessment.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently screened by two authors (MB, RD) and two advanced graduate students. ... All potentially eligible articles were independently assessed in full text by three authors (MB, RD, FS) and two advanced graduate students.
elements.reason: Independence of reviewers is explicitly stated for both screening stages.

elements.quote: Discrepancies (29%) were resolved through discussion and consensus. ... Disagreements were resolved by consensus.
elements.reason: Disagreement resolution via discussion and consensus is described for both screening stages.

elements.quote: For studies with unavailable full-texts, authors were contacted or articles purchased.
elements.reason: Contacting authors is reported, but in the context of obtaining full texts rather than confirming eligibility information from investigators; eligibility confirmation processes are not fully described.

elements.quote: Four articles were excluded due to the Japanese language, as no Japanese-speaking associate was available in our laboratory.
elements.reason: Handling of non-English articles is partially described (exclusion when translation was impossible), but no general translation methods for eligible non-English articles are reported.

elements.quote: After screening 2977 articles, the artificial intelligence 'Rayyan' was used for further screening. Rayyan has been proved as a reliable tool for abstract sreening [38, 214, 246]. In this review, we found a substantial overall agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.78; [160]).
elements.reason: Use of the Rayyan automation tool in abstract screening is described, including agreement statistics.
No evidence of externally derived classifiers being used in the selection process.
No evidence of internally derived classifiers being used.
No machine-learning prioritisation or stopping rules are reported; Rayyan was used for screening but not as a prioritisation tool with stopping rules.
No crowdsourcing platforms were used.
No previously screened datasets used to eliminate records are reported.

elements.quote: For data extraction, an a priori-developed tool was piloted on the first five articles.
elements.reason: The data extraction section describes the tool and data items but never states how many reviewers extracted data from each report.

elements.quote: Extracted data comprised study identification, study and measurement characteristics...
elements.reason: Independence of data extractors is not reported for the data extraction step; independence is only described for screening and risk of bias assessment (text_13).

elements.quote: Discrepancies (29%) were resolved through discussion and consensus.
elements.reason: Disagreement resolution is described only for screening and risk of bias, not for the data extraction/collection process itself.

elements.quote: Seven studies were excluded because researchers could not be contacted and articles could not be be purchased.
elements.reason: This implies attempts were made to contact study investigators, but no process for obtaining or confirming data from investigators is described.
No automation tools used in data collection are described in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Four articles were excluded due to the Japanese language, as no Japanese-speaking associate was available in our laboratory.
elements.reason: Translation of non-English articles is not described; Japanese articles were excluded rather than translated, and no translation methods for other languages are reported.
No software for extracting data from figures is mentioned in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Among the included studies, none were excluded for using the same sample, as each study employed different ER measures.
elements.reason: A brief statement about same-sample studies is given, but no decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies between reports are described.

elements.quote: Extracted data comprised study identification, study and measurement characteristics (study design, publication type), sample characteristics (age, gender, ethnicity, child/family characteristics), definition/model of ER, measurement of ER and psychometric properties of ER measurements (reliability, validity, objectivity).
elements.reason: The data items/outcome domains sought are listed (psychometric properties: reliability, validity, objectivity; plus study/sample characteristics), and text_14 names the primary outcome ('reporting of psychometric properties in behavioral and physiological ER measures'), but the domains are not formally defined in the Methods.
No time frame of measurement (e.g., time points, follow-up periods) for outcome domains is reported in the retrieved evidence.
The manuscript does not state whether all compatible results within each outcome domain (all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.
No process for selecting which compatible results to collect is described in the retrieved evidence.
Although text_6 mentions modifications to pre-registered eligibility criteria and search strategy, no changes to outcome-domain inclusion or definitions with rationales are reported.
No changes to processes for selecting results within outcome domains are reported.
The primary outcome is named (text_14), but no rationale for prioritising particular outcomes for interpreting conclusions is provided.

elements.quote: Extracted data comprised study identification, study and measurement characteristics (study design, publication type), sample characteristics (age, gender, ethnicity, child/family characteristics), definition/model of ER, measurement of ER and psychometric properties of ER measurements (reliability, validity, objectivity).
elements.reason: The Data Extraction section lists and defines the variables for which data were sought, including study, sample, measurement, and psychometric characteristics.

No evidence describes assumptions made about missing or unclear study information during data extraction; the Limitations section notes missing ethnicity/income data but does not describe assumptions made in handling such missingness.

elements.quote: For data extraction, an a priori-developed tool was piloted on the first five articles.
elements.reason: A data extraction tool is mentioned and its piloting described, but the tool is not named or cited (e.g., no reference to a published framework or citation for which data items to collect).

elements.quote: The revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool [227] was applied to randomized controlled trials... For non-randomized and observational quantitative studies, the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) Quality Assessment Tool was used [232].
elements.reason: Both risk-of-bias tools (RoB 2 and EPHPP) and their assignment by study design are explicitly specified.

elements.quote: In the EPHPP tool, domains are rated as strong, moderate, or weak and a global rating is assigned based on the number of weak domains. RoB 2 classifies studies as low risk, some concerns, or high risk, depending on the highest risk level across domains.
elements.reason: Domains are referenced (e.g., 'Selection of the reported results', blinding, dropout) but the full set of domains/items assessed by each tool is not comprehensively listed.

elements.quote: a global rating is assigned based on the number of weak domains. RoB 2 classifies studies as low risk, some concerns, or high risk, depending on the highest risk level across domains.
elements.reason: Overall risk-of-bias judgements are made and the rules for deriving them are reported for both tools.

elements.quote: Within the EPHPP rating scheme, we excluded the 'Study Design' section, as it was not applicable to non-RCT studies.
elements.reason: An adaptation to the EPHPP tool (exclusion of the Study Design section) is explicitly described.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool is reported; only existing tools (RoB 2, EPHPP) were used.

elements.quote: Risk of bias assessments were also conducted by the three authors (MB, RD, FS) and trained graduate students. Any discrepancies in ratings were discussed until consensus was reached.
elements.reason: Number of assessors, independence (independent assessment implied by discrepancy discussion), and consensus-based disagreement resolution are reported; interrater agreement statistics (kappa values) further support this.
No evidence describes contacting study investigators to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information.
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment are mentioned; the assessment was performed manually by reviewers.

elements.quote: The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment.
elements.reason: The methods specify the effect measure for the primary synthesis (proportions via logit-transformed random-effects meta-analysis). However, other effect measures used in presentation of results, such as Cohen's h for subgroup differences (text_22, text_26) and Cramér's V for Fisher's exact tests, are not specified in the methods section, so the specification is incomplete across all outcomes.
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect sizes (e.g., conventions for small/moderate/large effects) and their rationale are reported in the retrieved evidence.
No methods for re-expressing synthesized results using another effect measure are described in the retrieved evidence.
The choice of effect measure (logit-transformed proportions) is described but no justification for choosing it is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Studies were included according to the PICOS criteria [177]. Eligible studies included participants from birth to 15 years and 11 months. Studies were required to use at least one ER measurement and report ER as an outcome variable.
elements.reason: Eligibility criteria (PICOS) are described, and text_12 reports exclusion reasons (e.g., 'Other exclusions were based on ineligible age groups, absence of an ER outcome measure, secondary data, or insufficient detail on ER measurement'), while text_5 explains that only behavioral observation and physiological studies were included in this synthesis. However, an explicit description of the process used to decide which studies were eligible for each synthesis (e.g., tabulating study characteristics against planned groups) is not provided.

elements.quote: To facilitate comparison across studies, RoB 2 ratings were converted into a numerical format consistent with the EPHPP system (1 = low risk, 2 = some concerns, 3 = high risk). ... Data preparation and descriptive statistics were conducted in IBM SPSS Statistics (version 29).
elements.reason: Data conversion of RoB 2 ratings and data preparation software are described, but handling of missing summary statistics or other data preparation steps for synthesis is not reported.

elements.quote: Types of measures for ER based on behavioral observations and physiological measurements are described in the Supplementary Material (Tables 1a-1e and 2a-2e). ... the task of how the emotion is triggered is described first, followed by the duration of this task, the coding manuals used to measure ER, information on reliability, validity and objectivity and the citations and number of studies using the emotion eliciting task.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes the supplementary tables (1a-1e, 2a-2e) and the data fields included in them for behavioral observations and physiological measurements.

elements.quote: As shown in Fig. 3, studies focusing on younger age groups predominantly used behavioral observation measures, whereas studies involving older age groups favored physiological measurements.
elements.reason: A figure (Fig. 3) is referenced in the Results, but the Methods section contains no description of graphical methods used to display results of individual studies or syntheses.

elements.quote: Based on these values, measures were organized into broader age groups (neonates, infants, toddlers, preschool, school-aged children and teens) according to the American Academic of Pediatrics [6]. These broader categories were further divided into narrower age groups of 12 months categories. Within these 12 months categories the measures are organized according to the examined emotions
elements.reason: The basis for grouping/ordering studies within the tables (age groups per AAP categories, then 12-month categories, then examined emotions) is clearly reported.
No non-standard graphs are reported in the retrieved evidence; the only referenced figure (Fig. 3) appears to be a standard display, so no rationale for non-standard graphs is required.
No software package or version used for the meta-analysis or statistical tests is reported anywhere in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was performed, so the conditional requirement about describing an alternative because meta-analysis was not possible does not apply.

elements.quote: estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment
elements.reason: The model (random-effects) is explicitly reported for the meta-analysis of proportions.

elements.quote: a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment
elements.reason: The statistical method (logit transformation, inverse-variance weighting, Hartung-Knapp adjustment) is described.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q and the I 2 statistic.
elements.reason: Methods to identify and quantify statistical heterogeneity (Cochran's Q, I²) are explicitly reported.
The between-study variance estimator (e.g., DerSimonian-Laird, Paule-Mandel) for the random-effects model is not specified; only Hartung-Knapp adjustment is mentioned.

elements.quote: with inverse-variance weighting and Hartung-Knapp adjustment
elements.reason: The Hartung-Knapp adjustment specifies the method used for confidence intervals of summary effects in the random-effects model.
No other random-effects implementation details (e.g., transformation back from logit scale, exact variance estimator) are reported.

elements.quote: a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with inverse-variance weighting
elements.reason: No Bayesian meta-analysis was performed; a frequentist random-effects approach was used.
No methods for handling statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study (e.g., multilevel models, robust variance) are described in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Pooled effect estimates for specific reliability or validity indices were not calculated, as the available data were limited to the subset of studies reporting these psychometric indices (61% of all 516 studies). Because the reporting of such indices was not systematic across the literature, the resulting dataset may not have been fully representative of the broader evidence base. Consequently, any pooled estimates derived from this subset may have been biased
elements.reason: Planned syntheses (pooling of specific reliability/validity indices) judged inappropriate are identified with explicit reasons.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were conducted by age group and measurement type, with between-group differences evaluated using Q-tests. Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the meta-analytic estimates of the overall proportion of studies reporting psychometric properties.
elements.reason: Methods to explore heterogeneity (subgroup analyses by age group and measurement type, Q-tests, sensitivity analyses) are explicitly described in the Methods.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were conducted by age group and measurement type, with between-group differences evaluated using Q-tests.
elements.reason: Factors (age group, measurement type) and their levels (e.g., risk-of-bias low/moderate/high; age groups) are specified; expected direction of effect modification is partly indicated via hypotheses (e.g., reliability reported more than validity), though explicit directional expectations for each subgroup are not fully stated.

elements.quote: the main meta-analysis was repeated within subgroups defined by risk-of-bias ratings (low, moderate, high). To examine whether studies reporting psychometric properties differed from those that did not, studies were dichotomized based on whether at least one psychometric property was reported.
elements.reason: Analyses clearly use study-level variables (subgroups defined by study-level characteristics such as risk-of-bias rating, age group, measurement type).

elements.quote: with between-group differences evaluated using Q-tests
elements.reason: The method for comparing subgroup effects (Q-tests; also Fisher's exact tests and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for other comparisons) is reported.

elements.quote: Group differences were analyzed using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for continuous variables (e.g., sample size, gender, and ethnicity proportions), due to skewed data distributions, and chi-square tests (or Fisher's exact tests, where appropriate) for categorical variables (e.g., measurement type, age group, child characteristics, language, study design, and country group).
